clusters.label: PMU_DROOP
clusters.representative_signature: PMU_DROOP | PMU: Brown-out threshold crossed ; FW: Watchdog timeout ; SYSTEM: SoC reset asserted ; PMU: Regulator current limit hit ; PMU: Fast droop event

hypotheses.root_cause: The VCORE regulator hit its 2000 mA current limit (OCP) and folded back. That caused a fast droop from 850 to 611 mV and crossed the 750 mV brown-out threshold. The brown-out started a watchdog. Nothing cleared it, so it expired 3733 ms later and asserted SoC reset (reason=BROWNOUT_WDOG).
hypotheses.rationale: Causal chain: VCORE current spike past the 2000 mA limit (4.432 s) -> regulator current-limit foldback -> fast droop 850->611 mV, cause=regulator_limit (4.448 s) -> brown-out threshold of 750 mV crossed (4.457 s) -> watchdog started by the brown-out, never cleared even though the rail recovered (~4.56 s) and firmware kept running -> watchdog timeout after wd_ms=3733 = 8190-4457 (8.190 s) -> SoC reset BROWNOUT_WDOG (8.192 s). The PMU log matches the RC_REGULATOR_LIMIT signature exactly: an explicit "Regulator current limit hit i_limit_ma=2000" line 16 ms before the droop, and the droop itself is tagged cause=regulator_limit. The other possible causes were each ruled out by a different specialist. There are no load_step or di/dt markers (rules out RC_LOAD_STEP_SPIKE). There is no ringing or undershoot, and the rail recovered cleanly within about 100 ms (rules out RC_INSUFFICIENT_DECOUPLING). Firmware shows no DVFS changes or workload bursts, and thermal shows a flat 53–57 °C with no power-burst line (rules out RC_WORKLOAD_BURST and the thermal causes). DDR shows no traffic burst and no damage after the event (rules out RC_DMA_BURST_OVERFLOW). The firmware specialist found that wd_ms equals the time since the brown-out exactly, and firmware heartbeats continued the whole time. So the reset was set off by the brown-out, not by a firmware hang. The historian's similar incidents are all THERMAL_TRIP or NOC runs and don't match. I'm keeping confidence below 0.85 for two reasons. First, the cause of the current going over 2 A wasn't captured, because telemetry samples too slowly to see it. Second, the 2 A limit hasn't been checked against the VCORE spec. A normal peak of about 1.4 A leaves only about 30% headroom, which suggests the limit is set too low or the regulator is undersized. (1 of 4 specialists pointed at this cause.)
recommended_actions: Check the VCORE OCP setting (i_limit_ma=2000) against the rail's spec and the SoC's worst-case current. Rerun with the limit raised, for example to 2.5–3 A, and confirm the droop and brown-out don't come back.

Put a scope or current probe on VCORE, triggered on the regulator's current-limit flag, to capture the transient that crosses 2 A. Fast PMU telemetry would also work. This tells us what is drawing the current.
Dump the regulator's PMBus/OCP status, fold-back mode and LLC registers when the event happens. This run had no register dumps.
Review the brown-out watchdog design. Find out why the watchdog started by the brown-out isn't cleared once VCORE comes back within spec, and whether firmware should acknowledge the brown-out.
Run a margin sweep: different workloads at reduced OCP limits to measure the actual headroom.

trace.output: PMU: At 4.448s VCORE dropped fast from 850 to 611 mV with cause=regulator_limit, then the 750 mV brown-out threshold was crossed at 4.457s. What load-current step or DVFS transition came right before the droop? Did the regulator hit its current limit (OCP) or a slew limit? Did VCORE recover after the event or stay below threshold until reset? Check the regulator configuration (current limit, droop/LLC settings) against the spec.; FW: The watchdog timed out at 8.190s (wd_ms=3733), which lines up exactly with the brown-out at 4.457s. Did firmware hang because of the brown-out, for example a CPU stall or corrupted state at undervoltage? Or was firmware already stuck or running a heavy workload (DVFS request, power-virus-like burst) that caused the current spike at about 4.44s? List the firmware activity and any frequency or voltage change requests from 4.3 to 4.46s.; THERMAL: Similar past incidents were THERMAL_TRIP caused by RC_WORKLOAD_BURST, fan profile or heatsink problems. Around 4.4s, were temperatures high or rising quickly? Was there a thermal throttle or a missing throttle, or was leakage high enough to push VCORE current toward the regulator limit? Did the fan or cooling state change?; DDR: Was there a burst of DDR or memory traffic (training, refresh storm, large DMA) around 4.40 to 4.45s that could have contributed to a VCORE load step? Also, were there DDR errors after the droop at 4.457s that suggest it was a downstream victim of the brown-out?
trace.note: The chain of events is clear: VCORE fast droop (regulator_limit) leads to brown-out, then a watchdog timeout, then SoC reset. PMU owns the failing rail and the regulator limit. FW needs checking to tell whether the watchdog was a downstream effect or whether a firmware-driven DVFS change or workload caused the current step. THERMAL is a common upstream cause, and the similar past incidents point to workload-burst thermal problems and leakage. DDR (one of the more active subsystems) could explain the load step or be a downstream victim. PCIE and NOC are lower priority.

- RC_REGULATOR_LIMIT: Regulator reaches its current limit and folds back  (tell-tales: regulator current limit hit, cause=regulator_limit, i_limit)
